monitored_text: Resources / Materials / Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 16 min read Published July 16, 2026 Updated October 30, 2026 Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) is a thermoplastic elastomer used in wheels, seals, footwear parts, cable jackets, films, hoses, and molded industrial components. Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) combines plastic melt processability with rubber-like elasticity, giving the material flexibility, rebound behavior, abrasion resistance, and shape recovery after repeated deformation. TPU belongs to the polyurethane family and contains hard segments that support strength, plus soft segments that support elasticity. Grade chemistry controls hardness, oil resistance, hydrolysis resistance, and low-temperature flexibility. Covestro lists Desmopan and Texin TPU grades across 60 to 98 Shore A and 30 to 75 Shore D hardness ranges. TPU production uses injection molding, extrusion, blow molding, film casting, coating, calendaring, and additive manufacturing, depending on the target part geometry. Thermoplastic behavior lets TPU soften during heating, flow into a mold or die, then harden again after cooling, which separates it from crosslinked rubber. Industrial relevance comes from balanced toughness, tear resistance, wear resistance, chemical resistance, and flexible performance under repeated movement. TPU appears in automotive interiors, medical tubing, sports equipment, electronics protection, conveyor belts, gaskets, and precision parts where flexible durability matters. Material selection depends on the hardness target, service temperature, contact fluids, part thickness, and processing route for the finished component. What Is Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU)? Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) is a melt-processible thermoplastic elastomer that combines plastic processing behavior with rubber-like flexibility. TPU belongs to Thermoplastic Elastomers (TPE), a material group that delivers thermoplastic behavior and elastomeric properties in one polymer family. TWI defines Thermoplastic Elastomers (TPE) as copolymers or compounds with thermoplastic and elastomeric properties. TPU works as an engineering plastic because it provides abrasion resistance, tear strength, oil resistance, grease resistance, flexibility, and durable mechanical performance. SpecialChem describes TPU as a melt-processable thermoplastic elastomer with high durability and flexibility. Hard and soft polymer segments give TPU its hybrid structure, where rigid segments support strength and soft segments support elasticity. TPU suits injection molding, extrusion, films, coatings, and 3D printing for parts that require flexible strength under repeated use. What Is Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) Material Made of? Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) is synthesized from three primary raw materials a polyol soft segment, a diisocyanate hard segment, and a short-chain diol or diamine chain extender. Polyols come from polyester or polyether sources, and diisocyanates are commonly MDI, methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, or aliphatic diisocyanates (such as hexamethylene diisocyanate). The soft segments provide flexibility and low-temperature performance, contributing to elastic recovery and elongation at break. The hard segments form rigid, hydrogen-bonded domains that deliver tensile strength and dimensional stability. The ratio of soft to hard segments directly controls the final Shore hardness, ranging from Shore A 60 to Shore D 80, depending on formulation. Polyester-based TPU gives stronger abrasion resistance and oil resistance for mechanical parts. Polyether-based TPU gives better hydrolysis resistance and low-temperature flexibility for wet or outdoor service conditions. Chain extenders adjust molecular weight, hard segment spacing, and final mechanical performance across TPU grades. What Is the full form of Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU)? "Thermoplastic Polyurethane" is the full form of the acronym "TPU," where each word describes a defining chemical or physical characteristic of the material. "Thermoplastic" indicates the material softens reversibly upon heating, and "polyurethane" identifies the urethane linkage, NHCOO, backbone formed during polymerization. TPU is categorized as a thermoplastic elastomer because it combines the melt processability of thermoplastics with the elastic deformation behavior of vulcanized rubber, without requiring irreversible crosslinking. The material returns to its original shape after deformation, a defining trait of the thermoplastic elastomer classification. Reversible softening allows TPU to be injection molded, extruded, and reprocessed under controlled heating conditions. Polyurethane chemistry gives TPU strong abrasion resistance, tear strength, and bonding ability across films, coatings, and molded parts. The acronym TPU directly reflects the material's dual identity as a heat-processable polymer and an elastic engineering material. Is TPU Considered a Thermoplastic Elastomer? Yes, TPU is considered a thermoplastic elastomer because it combines thermoplastic processing with rubber-like elasticity. TPU belongs within Thermoplastic Elastomers (TPE), a polymer group that softens under heat and regains solid form after cooling. The material stretches, bends, and returns toward its original shape after deformation, which supports flexible part performance. Common elastomeric applications include seals, gaskets, shoe soles, cable jackets, protective films, and flexible automotive parts. Industrial relevance comes from TPU durability, abrasion resistance, tear strength, and process compatibility through injection molding and extrusion. TPU remains a strong material choice for flexible engineering parts that require a thermoplastic elastomer . What Are the Main Properties of Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU)? The main properties of Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) are listed below. Flexibility: TPU maintains rubber-like flexibility across a Shore hardness range from Shore A 60 to Shore D 80, adapting to rigid and soft-grade applications through formulation adjustments of the hard and soft segment ratios. Abrasion Resistance: TPU outperforms natural rubber and many engineering plastics in abrasion resistance, making it suitable for high-wear surfaces (conveyor belts and industrial wheels). Chemical Resistance: TPU resists oils, greases, fuels, and many solvents, depending on whether polyester or polyether chemistry is used in the soft segment. Tensile Strength: Tensile strength values for TPU range from 25 MPa to 70 MPa, depending on hardness grade and segment composition. Elastic Recovery : TPU recovers its original shape after repeated deformation cycles, a performance trait critical in seals, diaphragms, and flexible couplings. Low-Temperature Performance: Polyether-based TPU grades retain flexibility at temperatures as low as -60°C, suitable for cold-environment applications. Transparency: Certain TPU grades are optically clear, enabling applications in protective films, screen protectors, and medical device windows. What Mechanical Properties Make TPU Suitable for Engineering Applications? The mechanical properties that make TPU suitable for engineering applications are listed below. High Tensile Strength: TPU achieves tensile strength from 25 MPa to 70 MPa, providing structural integrity in load-bearing components (drive belts and flexible couplings). Elongation at Break: TPU stretches from 300% to 800% elongation at break before failure, giving it deformation tolerance far exceeding rigid engineering plastics. Tear Resistance: TPU exhibits tear resistance values from 30 kN/m to 150 kN/m, protecting components from edge-initiated cracking in dynamic-load environments. Compression Set Resistance: TPU maintains shape recovery after sustained compressive loading, a key requirement in gaskets, o-rings, and cushioning elements. Hardness Range: Shore hardness spans from Shore A 60 to Shore D 80, covering everything from soft over-molded grips to rigid structural profiles. Fatigue Resistance: TPU withstands repeated mechanical cycling without significant crack propagation, supporting its use in flexing hoses and articulated joints. Does Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) Resist Abrasion? Yes, TPU resists abrasion at a level that surpasses natural rubber, neoprene, and many engineering-grade plastics. The urethane hard-segment domains create a microstructure that dissipates surface friction energy without material loss at the macro level. In high-friction environments, TPU performs reliably in applications (industrial wheels, conveyor belts, hydraulic seals, and protective coatings on mining equipment). Abrasion resistance ratings for TPU are measured using the ISO 4649 method, with typical volume loss values below 90 mm³, significantly lower than rubber compounds in equivalent tests. Protective liners and equipment skins made from TPU extend service life in abrasive bulk-handling industries (aggregate processing and cement manufacturing). What Are the Different Types of Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) Materials? The different types of Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) materials are listed below. Polyester-Based TPU: Polyester TPU is synthesized using polyester polyols, delivering high tensile strength, oil resistance, and abrasion resistance. It is the preferred grade for mechanical and industrial applications (gears, seals, and drive belts) where chemical exposure to oils and fuels is common. Polyether-Based TPU: Polyether TPU uses polyether polyols (polytetramethylene glycol) as the soft segment, providing superior hydrolysis resistance, low-temperature flexibility, and microbial resistance. Medical devices, underwater equipment, and cold-storage applications specify polyether TPU for its moisture-stable performance. Polycarbonate-Based TPU: Polycarbonate TPU combines a polycarbonate polyol soft segment with standard diisocyanate chemistry, producing a grade with exceptional UV stability, heat resistance, and hydrolytic durability compared to standard polyester or polyether variants. Aliphatic TPU: Aliphatic TPU uses non-aromatic diisocyanates (HDI or IPDI) instead of MDI, producing a UV-stable, non-yellowing grade suited for exterior coatings, automotive clear coats, and optical films. Thermoplastic Polyurethane Foam Grades: Expanded or microcellular TPU foam grades provide cushioning, energy absorption, and acoustic dampening in footwear midsoles (such as Nike ZoomX and Adidas Boost) and sports padding. What Is the Difference Between Polyester TPU and Polyether TPU? Polyester TPU and Polyether TPU differ primarily in their soft-segment chemistry, which directly governs hydrolysis behavior, flexibility, and environmental durability. Polyester TPU delivers superior mechanical strength and oil resistance, making it ideal for industrial wear applications. Polyether TPU prioritizes moisture resistance and low-temperature flexibility, making it the standard for medical and aquatic applications. The difference between Polyester TPU and Polyether TPU is shown in the table. Which Industries Use Specialty TPU Grades? The industries that use specialty TPU grades are listed below. Medical Device Manufacturing: Aliphatic and polyether TPU grades meet biocompatibility standards (ISO 10993 and USP Class VI), used in catheter tubing, blood-contacting components, and wound care films. Automotive Industry: Polycarbonate and aliphatic TPU grades serve in paint protection films, instrument panel skins, weatherstripping, and airbag covers requiring UV stability and long-term elasticity. Footwear Manufacturing: Microcellular polymer foam grades (such as polyether block amide and expanded TPU) form midsoles, outsoles, and toe caps in athletic and safety footwear for energy return and durability. Electronics and Cable Manufacturing: Flame-retardant TPU grades jacket data cables, power cords, and wiring harnesses, meeting UL 94 V-0 and RoHS compliance requirements. Sports and Outdoor Equipment: UV-stable aliphatic TPU grades protect ski boots, helmet shells, and inflatable sports equipment exposed to UV radiation and mechanical impact. Defense and Industrial Coatings: Specialty aromatic TPU coatings protect military vehicle panels, industrial hoses, and offshore platform components from abrasion, corrosion, and chemical exposure. For instance, selecting a polyester grade for its high wear resistance can completely backfire if the part faces humid service conditions, causing premature hydrolytic failure. Optimizing for design for manufacturing (DFM) means aligning the chemical foundation (polyester vs. polyether) and specific processing boundaries (such as injection pressures and strict pre-drying rules) directly with the environmental reality of the final product." Audrius Zidonis PhD Principal Engineer at Zidonis Engineering Is TPU Commonly Used in Medical Device Manufacturing? Yes, TPU is commonly used in medical device manufacturing. Polyether-based and aliphatic TPU grades satisfy biocompatibility requirements under ISO 10993 and USP Class VI classifications, enabling their use in blood-contacting and implant-adjacent applications. Medical-grade TPU is found in catheter shafts, balloon catheters, IV tubing, wound dressings, and peristaltic pump tubing, where flexibility, kink resistance, and sterilization compatibility (EtO, gamma, e-beam) are required. The material bonds readily to other substrates through over-molding, allowing manufacturers to create multi-durometer devices with rigid connectors and soft flexible sections in a single manufacturing step. Polyether TPU's resistance to hydrolysis maintains mechanical integrity during steam sterilization cycles and prolonged fluid exposure. What Is TPU Filament Used for in 3D Printing? TPU filament is used for flexible 3D printed parts that need bend resistance, impact absorption, and elastic recovery. TPU filament is a flexible thermoplastic polyurethane material that feeds through a 3D printer, melts inside the hot end, and forms soft parts after cooling. The filament bends without cracking, making it suitable for parts exposed to movement, pressure, and repeated handling. Common applications include phone cases, watch straps, shoe components, grips, seals, gaskets, protective covers, vibration dampers, and cable sleeves. Wearable products benefit from TPU filament because the material supports skin-contact flexibility and shape recovery during daily use. Functional 3D printed parts use TPU filament when rigid plastics lack flexibility or shock absorption. Product teams use TPU for prototypes that test fit, comfort, compression, and movement before final production. Industrial use covers soft tooling, protective pads, flexible hinges, custom caps, and machine-contact parts. Print settings require a slower speed, direct-drive extrusion, and controlled retraction because flexible filament compresses inside the feed path. TPU filament remains valuable for flexible, durable, and functional components in 3D Printing . How Does TPU Filament Differ from Standard 3D Printing Materials? TPU filament differs from standard 3D printing materials in its elastic deformation behavior, print speed requirements, and mechanical output. PLA and ABS are rigid and brittle by comparison, fracturing under the deformation loads that TPU absorbs elastically. The table below compares TPU filament with PLA, ABS, and PETG across key performance and process variables. The difference between TPU Filament and standard 3D printing materials is shown in the table below. How to Print Successfully with TPU Filament? To print successfully with TPU filament, follow the seven steps below. Set a slower print speed. TPU prints best at 20 to 35 mm/s because slow movement reduces filament buckling and flow instability. Slower printing improves layer bonding for flexible parts. Use a direct drive extruder. A direct drive extruder keeps the filament path short from the drive gear to the hot end. Short feed distance improves control over soft filament during extrusion. Adjust nozzle temperature. TPU commonly prints from 210°C to 240°C, depending on the filament grade. Higher temperature improves flow, while excessive heat causes stringing. Reduce retraction settings. Low retraction reduces stretching and compression inside the feed path. Excessive retraction causes jams, gaps, and inconsistent extrusion. Prepare the print bed. A clean PEI sheet, glue stick, or textured build plate improves first-layer grip. Bed temperature from 40°C to 60°C supports stable adhesion. Dry the filament before printing. TPU absorbs moisture from the air, which causes popping, bubbles, and rough surfaces during extrusion. Dry storage protects print quality and material strength. Test settings before final parts. A small calibration print verifies flow rate, temperature, stringing, and layer bonding. Successful flexible parts depend on stable printer settings for TPU filament. Can TPU Filament be Used for Flexible Parts? Yes, TPU filament is used for flexible parts because the material bends, stretches, and recovers its shape after deformation. TPU filament supports additive manufacturing parts that need movement, compression, and impact absorption. The material suits phone cases, wearable straps, seals, gaskets, grips, hinges, vibration pads, and protective covers. Elastic recovery helps printed parts return close to their original form after bending or pressure. Flexibility depends on Shore hardness, wall thickness, infill density, print speed, and extrusion control. TPU filament gives 3D printed parts stronger movement tolerance than rigid plastics used for static components. Lower Shore hardness grades create softer parts for comfort-focused products. Higher infill levels increase stiffness while preserving flexible behavior under repeated use. How Is Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) Processed in Manufacturing? Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) is processed through extrusion, injection molding, blow molding, calendering, and solution coating, using standard thermoplastic processing equipment without requiring chemical crosslinking agents. The material is supplied as dried pellets, which are fed into a heated processing machine where the TPU melts, flows, and is shaped into profiles, parts, films, or coatings. Extrusion produces continuous profiles (tubing, sheet, film, and wire jacketing), while injection molding produces discrete net-shape parts at high production volumes. TPU processing temperatures range from 180°C to 230°C, depending on grade, and pre-drying at 80°C to 110°C for 2 to 4 hours is required to prevent hydrolytic degradation during melt processing. The materials' recyclability allows production scrap to be reground and reintroduced into the feed stream without major property loss, supporting manufacturing efficiency at scale. Proper moisture control protects surface quality, melt stability, and mechanical strength during processing. Screw speed, residence time, and mold temperature affect flow behavior and final part consistency. TPU processing supports flexible production across industrial parts, films, tubing, and protective coatings. How Does Plastic Injection Molding Work with TPU? Plastic injection molding with TPU begins with pellet drying, where TPU resin is conditioned at 80°C to 110°C for 2 to 4 hours to reduce moisture below 0.02% before processing. Undried TPU produces hydrolytic chain scission during melt processing, resulting in surface defects, reduced molecular weight, and weakened mechanical properties in the molded part. Dried pellets are fed into the injection molding barrel, where screw rotation and barrel heaters melt the material at 190°C to 230°C. The melt is then injected into a closed steel mold under pressures from 20 MPa to 110 MPa, filling the cavity and packing the part to compensate for shrinkage. Mold temperatures from 20°C to 50°C promote surface finish quality and dimensional accuracy, after which the part is ejected and undergoes secondary operations (deflashing, overmolding, or assembly) as required. How Does Liquid Silicone Injection Molding Compare to TPU Molding? Liquid Silicone Injection Molding and TPU molding differ in material chemistry, flexibility, heat behavior, cycle control, and end-use performance. Liquid Silicone Rubber cures through heat inside the mold, while TPU melts in the barrel and solidifies after cooling in the mold. Yes, TPU is easier to process than liquid silicone rubber in injection molding for standard thermoplastic manufacturing environments. TPU uses conventional single-barrel injection molding equipment without the two-component metering, mixing, and injection systems that LSR processing requires. TPU cycle times from 15 to 60 seconds are faster than LSR cycle times from 30 to 120 seconds because TPU solidifies by cooling rather than by heat-activated chemical crosslinking. LSR tooling requires precision-controlled temperature zones and flash-free parting line management, adding tooling cost and process complexity beyond standard TPU mold requirements. Facilities already equipped for thermoplastic injection molding integrate TPU into existing production lines without capital investment in specialized LSR-specific equipment. Why Is TPU Preferred Over Traditional Synthetic-Rubber Materials? TPU is preferred over traditional synthetic rubber materials because TPU combines elastic recovery, abrasion resistance, tear strength, and thermoplastic processing in one material. Synthetic rubber requires curing or vulcanization, while TPU melts and reshapes through standard thermoplastic processing. The table below compares TPU and synthetic rubber across key performance characteristics. What Limitations Should Engineers Consider When Using TPU? The limitations engineers should consider when using TPU are listed below. Hydrolytic Degradation in Polyester Grades: Polyester-based TPU undergoes chain scission when exposed to sustained moisture, steam, or humid environments, reducing tensile strength and elasticity over time. Polyether-based grades address the limitation at a higher material cost. Elevated Temperature Performance Ceiling: TPU loses mechanical properties at sustained temperatures above 80°C to 100°C (depending on grade), making it unsuitable for high-temperature sealing or structural applications where silicone or PTFE is specified. Moisture Sensitivity During Processing: TPU absorbs atmospheric moisture and requires pre-drying at 80°C to 110°C for 2 to 4 hours before processing. Inadequately dried material produces surface splay, voids, and reduced molecular weight in finished parts. Compression Set at Elevated Temperature: TPU exhibits a permanent compression set when loaded at temperatures above 70°C for extended periods, limiting its use in high-temperature static sealing applications. UV Degradation in Aromatic Grades: Aromatic MDI-based TPU grades yellow and degrade mechanically under prolonged UV exposure. Aliphatic TPU grades resist UV degradation but carry a cost premium of 100% to 200% over aromatic equivalents. Processing Complexity at Low Shore Hardness: Soft TPU grades below Shore A 70 require direct drive extrusion, very low injection speeds, and precise temperature control to avoid melt instability, stringing, and dimensional variation. Is TPU More Expensive than Conventional Plastic Materials? Yes, TPU is more expensive than conventional plastic materials. Standard commodity TPU pellets are priced from [$2 to $6] per kilogram, compared to PLA at [$1.50 to $3] per kilogram and ABS at [$1.20 to $2.50] per kilogram, reflecting the higher cost of polyol and diisocyanate feedstocks. Specialty grades (aliphatic UV-stable, medical-grade, and polycarbonate-based TPU) reach [$8 to $20] per kilogram or higher, depending on biocompatibility certification and performance specifications. The cost premium is offset in engineering applications by TPU's longer service life, reduced replacement frequency, and elimination of secondary vulcanization processing steps required for equivalent rubber components. sections.text: What Is TPU Filament Used for in 3D Printing? TPU filament is used for flexible 3D printed parts that need bend resistance, impact absorption, and elastic recovery. TPU filament is a flexible thermoplastic polyurethane material that feeds through a 3D printer, melts inside the hot end, and forms soft parts after cooling. The filament bends without cracking, making it suitable for parts exposed to movement, pressure, and repeated handling. Common applications include phone cases, watch straps, shoe components, grips, seals, gaskets, protective covers, vibration dampers, and cable sleeves. Wearable products benefit from TPU filament because the material supports skin-contact flexibility and shape recovery during daily use. Functional 3D printed parts use TPU filament when rigid plastics lack flexibility or shock absorption. Product teams use TPU for prototypes that test fit, comfort, compression, and movement before final production. Industrial use covers soft tooling, protective pads, flexible hinges, custom caps, and machine-contact parts. sections.text: How Does TPU Filament Differ from Standard 3D Printing Materials? TPU filament differs from standard 3D printing materials in its elastic deformation behavior, print speed requirements, and mechanical output. PLA and ABS are rigid and brittle by comparison, fracturing under the deformation loads that TPU absorbs elastically. sections.heading: How to Print Successfully with TPU Filament?
sections.text: How to Print Successfully with TPU Filament? To print successfully with TPU filament, follow the seven steps below. Set a slower print speed. TPU prints best at 20 to 35 mm/s because slow movement reduces filament buckling and flow instability. Slower printing improves layer bonding for flexible parts. Use a direct drive extruder. A direct drive extruder keeps the filament path short from the drive gear to the hot end. Short feed distance improves control over soft filament during extrusion. Adjust nozzle temperature. TPU commonly prints from 210°C to 240°C, depending on the filament grade. Higher temperature improves flow, while excessive heat causes stringing. Reduce retraction settings. Low retraction reduces stretching and compression inside the feed path. Excessive retraction causes jams, gaps, and inconsistent extrusion. Prepare the print bed. A clean PEI sheet, glue stick, or textured build plate improves first-layer grip. Bed temperature from 40°C to 60°C supports stable adhesion. Dry the filament before printing. sections.heading: How Is Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) Processed in Manufacturing?
sections.text: How Is Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) Processed in Manufacturing? Thermoplastic Polyurethane (TPU) is processed through extrusion, injection molding, blow molding, calendering, and solution coating, using standard thermoplastic processing equipment without requiring chemical crosslinking agents. The material is supplied as dried pellets, which are fed into a heated processing machine where the TPU melts, flows, and is shaped into profiles, parts, films, or coatings. Extrusion produces continuous profiles (tubing, sheet, film, and wire jacketing), while injection molding produces discrete net-shape parts at high production volumes. TPU processing temperatures range from 180°C to 230°C, depending on grade, and pre-drying at 80°C to 110°C for 2 to 4 hours is required to prevent hydrolytic degradation during melt processing. The materials' recyclability allows production scrap to be reground and reintroduced into the feed stream without major property loss, supporting manufacturing efficiency at scale. sections.heading: How Does Plastic Injection Molding Work with TPU?
sections.text: How Does Plastic Injection Molding Work with TPU? Plastic injection molding with TPU begins with pellet drying, where TPU resin is conditioned at 80°C to 110°C for 2 to 4 hours to reduce moisture below 0.02% before processing. Undried TPU produces hydrolytic chain scission during melt processing, resulting in surface defects, reduced molecular weight, and weakened mechanical properties in the molded part. Dried pellets are fed into the injection molding barrel, where screw rotation and barrel heaters melt the material at 190°C to 230°C. The melt is then injected into a closed steel mold under pressures from 20 MPa to 110 MPa, filling the cavity and packing the part to compensate for shrinkage. Mold temperatures from 20°C to 50°C promote surface finish quality and dimensional accuracy, after which the part is ejected and undergoes secondary operations (deflashing, overmolding, or assembly) as required.

sections.heading: What Limitations Should Engineers Consider When Using TPU?
sections.text: What Limitations Should Engineers Consider When Using TPU? The limitations engineers should consider when using TPU are listed below. Hydrolytic Degradation in Polyester Grades: Polyester-based TPU undergoes chain scission when exposed to sustained moisture, steam, or humid environments, reducing tensile strength and elasticity over time. Polyether-based grades address the limitation at a higher material cost. Elevated Temperature Performance Ceiling: TPU loses mechanical properties at sustained temperatures above 80°C to 100°C (depending on grade), making it unsuitable for high-temperature sealing or structural applications where silicone or PTFE is specified. Moisture Sensitivity During Processing: TPU absorbs atmospheric moisture and requires pre-drying at 80°C to 110°C for 2 to 4 hours before processing. Inadequately dried material produces surface splay, voids, and reduced molecular weight in finished parts. Compression Set at Elevated Temperature: TPU exhibits a permanent compression set when loaded at temperatures above 70°C for extended periods, limiting its use in high-temperature static sealing applications.
